analysis.one_liner: Makes police chokeholds a federal criminal civil rights violation.
analysis.headline: Despite 127 House Democrats signed on as cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died in a House Judiciary subcommittee when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend a federal criminal civil rights law so that any pressure to a person's throat or windpipe that may hinder breathing — a chokehold — counts as an unlawful "punishment, pain, or penalty" by officials acting under color of law. That would give federal prosecutors a clearer criminal tool against officers who use neck restraints, a practice named for Eric Garner, who died in 2014 after a New York police officer choked him. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People stopped or arrested by police — especially Black Americans, who are disproportionately subjected to neck restraints and lethal force — gain a clearer federal criminal protection against chokeholds. Families of people killed or injured by neck restraint would gain a specific federal statute to point to, and federal prosecutors would no longer have to argue from scratch that a chokehold is a form of unlawful punishment.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the federal criminal civil rights statute (18 U.S.C. § 242) to state that any pressure to the throat or windpipe that may prevent or hinder breathing is a 'punishment, pain, or penalty' — making a chokehold by an official acting under color of law a federal criminal civil rights violation.

Because the definition reaches any pressure that 'may' hinder breathing rather than only holds explicitly labeled chokeholds, it closes a gap officers could otherwise argue around, and it does so without requiring any new agency or funding — it works through prosecutors already empowered under the existing statute.

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement officers and the departments they work for bear the cost: chokeholds would carry explicit federal criminal exposure under the civil rights statute, with the usual costs of investigation and prosecution falling on the Justice Department and taxpayers. Officers could face federal charges for conduct that today sits in a legal gray zone.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not actually ban chokeholds. It only declares that a chokehold counts as a 'punishment, pain, or penalty' under an existing criminal statute that requires willful misconduct — so it changes nothing unless a federal prosecutor chooses to bring a case, and federal prosecutions of officers for on-duty force are rare.

The wording is broad: 'any pressure to the throat or windpipe which may prevent or hinder breathing' could reach force well short of a deliberate chokehold, and officers are already criminally exposed under the same statute for excessive force, so critics could fairly call the amendment largely symbolic rather than a real new protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a specific, explicit federal criminal prohibition on a restraint technique that has killed people in police custody — is real but modest, because the statute still requires willful misconduct and depends on Justice Department willingness to prosecute. The cost to officers and departments is limited to genuinely unlawful use of neck restraints. The honest weakness is that the bill would not stop a single chokehold on its own; it only sharpens a tool after the fact. A stronger bill would have banned the practice outright and conditioned federal funding on compliance, as broader police reform proposals attempted.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee's crime subcommittee in October 2019 and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries introduced the bill on September 19, 2019, with two dozen original cosponsors including members of the Congressional Black Caucus.
The same day, it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee; on October 28, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security.
That subcommittee referral was the bill's last action: it never received a hearing, a committee markup, or a floor vote, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement officers and departments are better off, because they face no new federal criminal exposure for chokeholds. House Democratic leadership also avoided taking a recorded position that could have put some members on the spot.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police departments avoiding new federal liability

for.name: Hakeem Jeffries
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, recruiting two dozen original cosponsors.

for.name: 127 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the support of a majority of the House Democratic caucus.

against.name: Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee markup or hearing; it remained parked in the Crime subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican conference
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and none acted to move it out of committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 127 cosponsors were House Democrats — a majority of the 231-member caucus — while no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced far enough for a recorded vote.

industries.industry: Law enforcement (police departments and officer unions)
industries.note: Officers would gain explicit federal criminal exposure for applying pressure to the throat or windpipe, ending the gray zone around neck restraints. Police unions have historically opposed chokehold bans, and officers' interest in avoiding prosecution runs against the public's interest in protection from the practice.

Prosecutors would get a clearer statutory basis for charging chokeholds but also more cases they would be expected to bring, with the investigative and trial costs falling on the department. Their enforcement interest and the public's protection interest point the same way.
